prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening new precision tests of nature

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for B022 with Katori and Ye. All eight of us arrived at the same configuration from different starting points, but I do not rest the case on that count. I rest it on what I would ask of any instrument that flies or sits in a laboratory. There is a clear idea, Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which cancels the light shift while the lattice removes Doppler and recoil effects for many atoms at once. There is a long, patient programme of systematics control, taken to 10^-18 by Ye's group. There is independent reproduction and routine clock-to-clock comparison at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST. And there is a physics return already in hand: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, a many-body clock regime, and sharp limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter. In answer to the chair's own question on wording, I would accept either 'invention' or 'development' alone, but the citation I propose joins them because Katori's concept and Ye's record performance are the two decisive steps and the two names map onto them. The forward-looking clause answers the discovery-versus-tool objection that I and Eriksson and Kroll raised: the clocks are a way of observing nature at a new level, and the redshift and many-body results are already in the literature.
statement.case_against: The objections have not gone away and I do not want to pretend they have. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover the neighbouring steps, and a sceptic can call the lattice clock the next increment in one lineage. My answer is that the lattice architecture, many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength with a different error budget, is a distinct route and can be written into the citation, but I accept that Eriksson, Lindroth and Olsson are not fully persuaded. The scientific payoff beyond precision is so far upper limits and consistency checks; nothing new has been observed. Credit is not perfectly tidy: Lemonde and SYRTE, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom contributed, and Ye's share is partly the work of a large JILA team. I cannot verify priority from the packet and I say so plainly. Finally the redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the societal case is prospective.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B022 first because it opens new ways of observing nature, and he asks whether a two-name award is robust against claims from Lemonde, Hollberg, Gill and the ion-clock groups, while also disclosing a mild personal link through John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with your test of whether a result opens a new way of observing nature, and as a detector person I apply the same one. On credit, I have no primary evidence that would justify adding a third name, and I would not substitute one, because the contributions of Lemonde, Gill and Hollberg were to the neighbouring ingredients and not to the combination of lattice, magic wavelength and 10^-18 control. Whoever would add a name needs to say which of the two decisive steps that person owns. On your disclosure, I think disclosure is sufficient: you state no collaboration or supervisory tie to Katori or Ye, and a year in a laboratory during a PhD is a community link, not a stake. I would not ask for recusal and I would ask the committee to record it in the minutes.

responses.point: Lindroth resists widening the credit beyond Katori and Ye, but notes that the weighting between Katori's concept and the JILA record performance has to be settled, and she says the redefinition of the second leaves some members wanting to wait.
responses.response: I share your resistance to widening, and my answer to your round-1 question stands: I would not insist on adding anyone. On the weighting, I think it is settled by the citation itself, which names the invention of the lattice clock and its development to 10^-18, so that neither name is subordinate. On waiting for the redefinition, I disagree with waiting. A prize for a measurement should recognise reproduced, quantified performance, and the 10^-18 agreement across several laboratories is that. The redefinition depends on metrological committees and the readiness of the clock network, not on the physics being in doubt, and a Nobel prize has not generally waited for that kind of institutional step.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B018 to B022 but still describes it as an instrument and measurement achievement rather than the discovery of a new state or phenomenon, and worries it reads as the same territory as 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I concede your premise: this is not a new state of matter or a new phenomenon, and I said as much in round 1. But I do not think it is the same territory. In 2005 the prize honoured the comb as a ruler for optical frequencies, and in 2012 control of single quantum systems. The lattice clock is a different object, a many-atom quantum system whose systematics are understood well enough that its own many-body physics shows up in the error budget. As a theorist who checks that independent codes agree, you will recognise that standard: several laboratories agree at 10^-18 with different atoms and different methods. I would ask you to say whether the 'opening new precision tests of nature' clause is enough to meet your concern, and if not what you would put in the citation instead.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the lattice clock is a clue pulled out of nature by measurement, with the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and he proposes B020 or B028 as fallbacks.
responses.response: Your framing helps me and I would like the citation to carry it, which is why I accepted your wording with the forward-looking clause. I only partly agree on the fallbacks. B020 is the right principal alternative, but your own round-1 view and the other members' proposals for its names (Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, with or without Esslinger or Cirac) still disagree, so it cannot be built into a second part today without a fight over names. B028 has a real surprise but the pairing mechanism is unsettled, as Eriksson points out. I would keep both as alternatives and not as a joint prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge that it is, but Eriksson, Lindroth and Olsson keep this open.
Whether Katori and Ye is the complete and fair credit; I cannot verify priority for Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg and the JILA, PTB, SYRTE and NIST teams from the packet.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second; I do not, but Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth asked the question.

A second prize part: no one has proposed one, and B020 and B002 each need a settled credit list that I do not think we have. I am outside my expertise on B020, B028 and the condensed-matter candidates and rely on colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B022. For disclosure: I work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur and ranked B002 (IceCube) and B009 (kilonovae) in a neighbouring field, with no known tie to IceCube or its credited candidate. I note Kroll's disclosed link through John Hall's laboratory and consider disclosure sufficient. As chair I have counted only the written positions.
